justification: run-code is green (26 blocks, 14 executed) and I re-ran it five times specifically targeting the three threaded demos (id=blocked-write's busy-timeout race, id=wal-snapshot, and especially id=lock-cycle which uses Task.Run + Barrier(2) + ManualResetEventSlim for genuine two-thread lock contention): all five runs produced byte-identical output, including the SQLITE_BUSY messages on both sides of the deadlock demo. The Barrier/ManualResetEventSlim rendezvous genuinely pins the interleaving (A always takes RESERVED before B attempts its write, and both writers are released into their blocking calls together), so this is not a race dressed up as determinism; the design is sound and I found zero flakiness. I independently verified the two central isolation-level claims against primary sources: SQL Server's page states verbatim 'This option is the SQL Server default' for Read Committed, and the ON/OFF-by-default split is exact -- 'If READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT is set to OFF (the default on SQL Server), the Database Engine uses shared locks to prevent other transactions from modifying rows while the current transaction is running a read operation' and 'READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON is the default on Azure SQL Database and SQL database in Microsoft Fabric' -- both are exact-string matches to the article's quotes. PostgreSQL's page confirms 'Read Committed is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL' and the per-query-snapshot description ('a SELECT query... sees only data committed before the query began; it never sees either uncommitted data or changes committed by concurrent transactions during the query's execution') and the Repeatable Read snapshot description ('a snapshot as of the start of the first non-transaction-control statement in the transaction') are exact-string matches, as is the claim that PostgreSQL's own Repeatable Read forbids phantom reads even though the standard does not require it. I also individually re-fetched and checked, sentence by sentence, every other quoted claim in the piece: SQLite's isolation.html ('serializable'/'actually serializing the writes'/'single writer'), lang_conflict.html (ABORT preserves prior statements' changes and is 'the default behavior and the behavior specified by the SQL standard'), lockingv3.html (the five lock states, one RESERVED at a time, EXCLUSIVE excludes all others), rescode.html (SQLITE_BUSY wording), c3ref/busy_timeout.html ('sleeps for a specified amount of time'/'returns SQLITE_BUSY'), lang_transaction.html (autocommit), the Microsoft.Data.Sqlite connection-strings page (Default Timeout = 30s), and the SQL Server deadlock guide's T1/T2/r1/r2 shared-lock-vs-exclusive-lock example, all of which are exact or near-exact matches supporting the sentence they're attached to. Against that backdrop I found two real quote-integrity problems, one of them serious enough to be the deciding factor for this round: (1) a flatly fabricated quotation attributed to SQLite's WAL documentation -- the phrase does not appear on the cited page in any form, and (2) an undisclosed word-insertion inside a quotation mark in the deadlock section that makes SQL Server's docs appear to say something they don't say verbatim. Everything else -- the ACID/atomicity narrative, the CHECK-constraint/ROLLBACK demos, the anomaly table, the two SQLite two-connection isolation demos, the WAL mechanics themselves (as opposed to the one misattributed quote), and the deadlock wait-for-cycle -- is accurate, well-derived, and considerably deeper on the SQLite-specific mechanics (five-state locking, busy-timeout races, the asymmetry with SQL Server's victim-picking deadlock monitor) than any general treatment of ACID a reader would otherwise find, including PostgreSQL's and Microsoft's own pages, which don't compare the two engines side by side or demonstrate any of it with running two-connection code. Per the hard editorial rule that nothing may be fabricated, including quotes, the one verified fabricated attribution keeps this round from a passing score even though the surrounding technical content is strong; fixing it and the deadlock misquote is a fast, mechanical repair.

issues.location: 'How does write-ahead logging change durability and concurrency?' section, sentence right after the id=wal-snapshot output block: 'In WAL mode, A's `COMMIT` no longer waits on B at all: [WAL mode "permits simultaneous readers and writers... because changes do not overwrite the original database file, but rather go into the separate write-ahead log file"](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)'
issues.problem: Fabricated quotation. I fetched https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html directly and confirmed the word 'permits' does not appear anywhere on the page, and the phrase 'simultaneous readers and writers' does not appear either -- the quoted sentence, in this wording or any close variant, is not on the cited page. The page's actual language for this point is, in section 2.2 'Concurrency': 'Readers can exist in separate processes... Writers merely append new content to the end of the WAL file. Because writers do nothing that would interfere with the actions of readers, writers and readers can run at the same time,' and in the 'Advantages' list: 'WAL provides more concurrency as readers do not block writers and a writer does not block readers.' The underlying technical point the article is making is correct, but the sentence presented in quotation marks as SQLite's own words is invented.
issues.fixLooksLike: Replace the invented quotation with the page's real wording, e.g. link the claim to 'writers and readers can run at the same time' (2.2 Concurrency) or 'readers do not block writers and a writer does not block readers' (Advantages), or drop the quotation marks entirely and state the point in the article's own words with a plain citation link, the way the surrounding sentences about checkpointing already do.

issues.location: 'What happens when two transactions each wait on a lock the other holds?' section: '[SQL Server's deadlock guide](...) says the engine "terminates the current batch... rolls back the transaction of the deadlock victim, and returns error 1205,"'
issues.problem: Misquote: the source sentence (Deadlocks Guide, 'Handle deadlocks' section) reads 'it terminates the current batch, rolls back the transaction, and returns error 1205 to the application.' The words 'of the deadlock victim' are inserted into the middle of the quoted sentence without brackets, presenting invented text as if it were verbatim documentation. The inserted claim happens to be true in substance (the victim's transaction is what gets rolled back), but the quotation marks assert it is SQL Server's own wording, which it is not.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either bracket the insertion explicitly -- 'rolls back the transaction[, i.e. the deadlock victim's,] and returns error 1205' -- or drop it, since the preceding clause already establishes which transaction: 'terminates the current batch, rolls back the transaction, and returns error 1205 to the application.'

issues.location: Exercise 'Commit after an ignored error', solution paragraph: 'PostgreSQL's tutorial says that once a statement inside a transaction errors, the transaction is left in an aborted state, and "the only way to regain control... [is] rolling it back completely and starting again" (or a savepoint).'
issues.problem: The source sentence (3.4 Transactions in the PostgreSQL tutorial) is 'ROLLBACK TO is the only way to regain control of a transaction block that was put in aborted state by the system due to an error, short of rolling it back completely and starting again.' In the source, 'ROLLBACK TO' -- a savepoint rollback -- is what is called 'the only way,' and 'rolling it back completely and starting again' is the one exception ('short of') to that. The article's ellipsis+bracket reconstruction swaps which clause fills the 'only way ... is' slot, so the quotation marks assert something the source's grammar does not say at that point, even though the article's own parenthetical '(or a savepoint)' recovers the correct overall meaning (there are two ways out: full rollback, or ROLLBACK TO a savepoint).
issues.fixLooksLike: Quote the sentence whole, or restructure without brackets that reverse the subject, e.g.: PostgreSQL's tutorial calls ROLLBACK TO (a savepoint) 'the only way to regain control of a transaction block that was put in aborted state by the system due to an error, short of rolling it back completely and starting again' -- i.e. a savepoint, or a full ROLLBACK, are the two ways out.
